item.title: Asymptotically Good Quantum Codes with Addressable Transversal T Gates
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Explicit binary CSS codes achieve constant rate Ki=Θ(Ni) and linear distance Di=Θ(Ni) while supporting fully addressable transversal logical T gates via physical powers of T without Clifford corrections.

Grade 0.492 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Tongyin Lin, Bujiao Wu, Bin Cheng

Asks

Can an explicit family of asymptotically good binary quantum codes admit fully addressable transversal T gates?

Before

Transversal T achieved growing distance 2Ω(log⁡N) at constant rate (Wills 2026) or linear distance with vanishing rate (Hastings and Haah 2018), but not both simultaneously with addressability.

But

Asymptotic regime in code block length Ni→∞. Binary CSS code construction without stabilizer generator weight bounds.

Tools

Algebraic-geometry evaluation codes over F₁₀₂₄ · Binary embedding with fivefold overlap identities · Generalized Z₈-divisibility modules · Affine space minimum Hamming weight formulation

Abstract

Designing quantum codes with both transversal non-Clifford gates and good error-correcting parameters is an important goal in fault-tolerant quantum computation. Here, we construct an explicit family of binary CSS codes with constant rate and linear distance that admit fully addressable transversal T gates. Specifically, any prescribed tensor product of logical powers of T is implemented by a tensor product of physical powers of T, without any subsequent correction. Our construction combines algebraic-geometry codes with suitable binary embedding to obtain generalized divisibility of binary codes. This divisibility then enables fully addressable transversal T gates. Furthermore, we formulate the minimum binary embedding length problem as a minimum-weight problem over an affine space and numerically improve the constants in the asymptotic rate and relative-distance bounds.

item.title: Circuit-level benchmarks of GKP-concatenated qLDPC Codes
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Under a schedule-resolved circuit noise model, analog-informed BP–OSD decoding of GKP-concatenated qLDPC codes yields crossing estimates of σth≃0.212 (10.46 dB squeezing) for bivariate bicycle (BB) codes and 0.142 (13.94 dB squeezing) for tricycle codes.

Grade 0.469 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Yuan Yao, Ruipeng Xing, Jianshuo Gao, Xiao Yuan

Figure

Word logical error rate versus displacement noise width σ for BB and tricycle codes under the full propagated circuit model, showing analog-informed BP-OSD crossings at σth≃0.212 and 0.142, respectively.

Asks

How do structured quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) outer codes perform when concatenated with Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) modes under circuit-level noise and analog-informed decoding?

Before

A passive-linear-optical measurement-based GKP architecture with BB outer codes achieved a threshold of σgkp≃0.209 (10.6 dB) using foliated graph states and correlation-aware decoding.

But

Finite-size crossing estimates evaluated on selected finite-length code instances (N≤144 for BB, N≤108 for tricycle), not universal asymptotic code family thresholds.

Tools

Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) codes · Bivariate bicycle (BB) and tricycle qLDPC codes · Analog-informed BP-OSD decoding · Schedule-resolved circuit noise simulation

Abstract

Scalable fault-tolerant quantum error correction based on Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) codes requires finite-rate outer codes that can exploit analog GKP information under realistic circuit noise. However, quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) outer codes have not been systematically compared as candidates for circuit-level GKP concatenation. Here, we benchmark BB and tricycle codes using a unified simulation framework that progresses from code-capacity noise to repeated noisy syndrome extraction and schedule-resolved displacement propagation. Across all three noise models, analog-informed belief-propagation with ordered-statistics decoding (BP-OSD) yields higher finite-size crossing estimates than hard-decision decoding. In the full circuit model, the analog-informed crossings are \(σ_th≃0.212\) for the selected BB sequence and \(0.142\) for the tricycle sequence, corresponding to squeezing requirements of approximately \(10.46 dB\) and \(13.94 dB\), respectively. These results show that analog GKP information continues to improve decoding under circuit-level noise. Under the common simulation assumptions used here, the selected BB sequence also yields a higher finite-size crossing estimate than the selected tricycle sequence.

item.title: Beyond NISQ Assumptions: One-time Memory in the Classically Accessible Random-Oracle Model
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Simulation-secure one-time memory (OTM) using BB84 states achieves simulation advantage ≤(n+3)(3/4)n against quantum adversaries restricted to at most q≤2ℓ/2−1−1 classical random-oracle queries.

Grade 0.450 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers in 8 hours using 20 million noisy qubits” · Boyang Chen, Tianren Liu, Luojian Wei

Asks

Can an efficient one-time memory protocol be constructed under assumptions robust to early fault-tolerant quantum computers instead of shallow NISQ circuits?

But

Adversary can perform arbitrary quantum computation and long-term quantum storage but cannot query the random oracle coherently on superpositions.

Tools

Classically Accessible Random Oracle Model (CAROM) · BB84 state encodings · List-recovery reduction · Parallel repetition · Equality-test games

Abstract

Quantum information enables many cryptographic primitives that are impossible in the classical world. A line of works has developed cryptographic protocol under the assumption that quantum adversaries are restricted to noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) computing power, enabling strong one-time functionalities. But the advent of early fault-tolerant quantum computers eras will allow deeper logical quantum circuits, calling into questions the applicability of these NISQ-based assumptions. In this work, we adapt the classically accessible random oracle model (CAROM) as in [BDF+11] and [AK22], in which adversaries are only allowed to classically query the random oracle. The restriction is well motivated for NISQ quantum adversaries and may remain plausible in the presence of early fault-tolerant quantum computers. Then, we show that an efficient simulation-secure one-time memory (OTM) is possible under CAROM. Our protocol uses only BB84 states and has quadratic communication: for a λ-bit message and integer-valued parameters n=n(λ) and ℓ=ℓ(λ), the construction uses nℓ qubits and (n+2)λ classical bits, and for any quantum adversary with at most 2^(ℓ/2-1)-1 classical queries to the random oracle, its simulation advantage is at most (n+3)(3/4)ⁿ. Hence exponentially small simulation advantage in n.

item.title: QBX: A Compiler for 2-local Qubit Hamiltonian Simulation on Quantum Chiplets
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Reduces compiled circuit depth by 2.57× over Qiskit and 10.35× over t|ket⟩ for 2-local Hamiltonian simulation on quantum chiplets, while cutting compilation time 19.54× compared to 2QAN.

Grade 0.441 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “lattice surgery, logical qubit layout and compilation to a fault-tolerant instr…” · Zikun Li, Zhuoming Chen, Zhihao Jia

Figure

Normalized circuit depth relative to Qiskit across benchmarks as multi-chip module size scales from 3 to 16 chiplets, demonstrating increasing depth reduction advantages.

Asks

How can 2-local qubit Hamiltonian simulation circuits be compiled to minimize cross-chiplet communication depth and operation count on multi-chiplet quantum architectures?

Before

Domain-specific compiler 2QAN timed out on most large benchmarks due to O(m2n) routing and O(m4) scheduling, and chiplet compiler MECH produced 1.69× higher circuit depth.

But

Simulated hardware models; ancilla qubit allocation on chiplets is not automated; cross-chiplet and measurement error rates fixed at pcross/pon=7.4 and pmeas/pon=0.7.

Tools

Hierarchical qubit-to-chiplet mapping · METIS graph partitioning · Integer linear programming (CPLEX) · Highway multi-target controlled state generation · Pauli block scheduling

Abstract

2-local qubit Hamiltonian simulation, a fundamental task in quantum computing, is widely applied in various applications. This paper presents QBX, the first quantum compiler designed for 2-local qubit Hamiltonian simulation on quantum chiplet architectures. Existing general-purpose quantum compilers for chiplet architectures target quantum programs at the gate level and miss optimizations requiring high-level semantics of Hamiltonian simulation. Conversely, existing domain-specific compilers for Hamiltonian simulation are designed for monolithic architectures, and their limited scalability and inability to adapt to the heterogeneity of chiplet architectures lead to sub-optimal circuit outputs. QBX implements a scalable hierarchical approach to reduce both the amount and distance of cross-chiplet communications. It integrates the highway mechanism, a chiplet-oriented solution for efficient long-range qubit communication, to diminish cross-chiplet interaction costs. Furthermore, QBX efficiently aggregates 2-local Pauli strings into multi-target controlled gates, harnessing highways for deep optimization. Our evaluations show that QBX markedly outperforms both general-purpose and domain-specific compilers in circuit depth and operation count, while scaling to much larger 2-local Hamiltonian simulations.

item.title: The Fully Depolarizing Noise Conjecture for Entangled Physical States: A Twenty-Year Perspective
item.description:
Worth a look review — Correlated error conjecture posits that for any entangled physical qubits, the effective noise channel necessarily retains a joint fully depolarizing component of rate comparable to elementary two-qubit entangling gates, even when entanglement is created indirectly.

Grade 0.440 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Gil Kalai

Figure

Conceptual schematic distinguishing physically attainable states in a proposed quantum architecture from unphysical hypothetical states where conjectured noise properties are tested.

Asks

What structural constraints on correlated noise in entangled physical qubits could inherently obstruct quantum fault tolerance?

Before

Standard stochastic fault-tolerance models predict the largest joint fully depolarizing component for indirect entanglement (e.g. via an intermediate mediator qubit) has weight t2 rather than t.

But

Open theoretical conjecture; assumes noise correlates directly with physical entanglement rather than obeying standard weak-decay or independent error assumptions.

Tools

Fully Depolarizing Noise Conjecture (FDNC) · localizable entanglement analysis · quantum channel tomography · noise sensitivity analysis

Abstract

In this paper I revisit my 2006 conjecture on correlated errors in entangled physical qubits, originally proposed as a potential obstruction to quantum fault tolerance. The conjecture asserts that, in any physical implementation of a quantum computer, the effective noise channel acting on entangled physical qubits contains a joint fully depolarizing component, with a rate comparable to that of two-qubit gate errors. This hypothesized structural constraint goes beyond standard noise models and, if valid, would pose a significant challenge to scalable quantum fault tolerance. The conjecture remains open, but recent advances in experimental quantum computing bring it within reach of empirical testing on current devices. I also discuss two related directions in my critical study of quantum computation: the role of noise sensitivity and computational complexity in noisy intermediate-scale quantum systems, and the statistical analysis of experimental claims of quantum advantage. Finally, since this paper is written for a volume honoring Yuri Gurevich, I include some reflections on the ways in which my scientific and personal trajectory became intertwined with Yuri's.

item.title: Depth-Optimal Quantum Compilation
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Any single-qubit unitary can be synthesized to precision ε in constant depth using O(log1+δ⁡(1/ε)) clean ancillae, single-qubit gates {H,T}, and generalized Toffoli gates without Fan-Out. In the bounded-width gate model, synthesis achieves optimal depth Θ(log⁡log⁡(1/ε)).

Grade 0.440 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers in 8 hours using 20 million noisy qubits” · Francisca Vasconcelos

Asks

Can quantum computation be restricted to a fixed gate set without increasing circuit depth?

Before

Kim-Laakkonen online synthesis achieved constant T-depth using an O(log⁡(1/ε))-qubit catalyst, but without an end-to-end constant-depth unitary catalyst preparation.

But

Asymptotic in precision ε; bounded-width compilation achieves Θ(log⁡log⁡(1/ε)) depth instead of constant depth.

Tools

block encoding · oblivious amplitude amplification · Aaronson-Ambainis partial-to-full Hadamard conversion · structured Fourier circuits

Abstract

We achieve the first constant-depth circuit for arbitrary single-qubit gate synthesis. Unlike prior approaches, the construction is fully unitary and requires no pre-supplied catalyst. For any constant δ>0, it ε-approximates an arbitrary single-qubit gate using O(log^(1+δ)(1/ε)) clean ancillae, Hadamard and T single-qubit gates, O(log(1/ε))-width generalized Toffoli gates, and sublogarithmic-width Fan-Out gates. We further eliminate Fan-Out entirely, showing that Hadamard, T, and generalized Toffoli gates alone suffice for constant-depth synthesis. When restricted to the standard bounded-width gate model, our construction has depth O(loglog(1/ε)), and we prove a matching Ω(loglog(1/ε))-depth lower bound. Overall, we establish that Θ(loglog(1/ε))-depth is unavoidable with only bounded-width gates, yet allowing even logarithmic-width multi-qubit gates suffices to achieve constant-depth synthesis. These results also reveal new structure in shallow quantum circuit complexity. We give a depth-preserving real simulation of bounded-error decision computation, showing that every depth-d QAC circuit can be simulated in depth O(d) using only Hadamard, X, and generalized Toffoli gates. Thus arbitrary single-qubit rotations and complex amplitudes do not increase the bounded-error decision power of QAC, even at constant depth. In particular, this reduces the long-standing conjecture Parity∉QAC⁰ to proving a Parity lower bound against circuits consisting only of Hadamard, X, and generalized Toffoli gates. More generally, this real normal form exposes a direct correspondence between the standard shallow-depth quantum circuit hierarchy and a hierarchy of Forrelation circuits with restricted oracle families.

item.title: NxM-Version Programming for Quantum Software: High-Level Components across Frameworks and Engines
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Wrapping high-level routines across 5 quantum frameworks into Apache NiFi processors using OpenQASM 2.0 exchange enabled N×M multi-version execution, uncovering 3 real hardware and cloud-adapter defects.

Grade 0.425 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Fault-tolerant quantum computation by anyons” · Neilson Carlos Leite Ramalho, Higor Amario de Souza, Anthony Accioly, Valter Vieira de Camargo, Marcos Lordello Chaim

Figure

The N×M multi-version execution topology, mapping one test case across 3 framework builders to 3 quantum devices for 9 parallel execution paths that converge at an oracle.

Asks

What quantum programs can be expressed at the visual component level without manual circuit coding, and what does running all framework-engine combinations reveal?

But

Evaluated on small Grover and adder circuits; 4-qubit Grover outputs approached random chance (probabilities of 0.01–0.19) due to hardware noise; shared Qiskit transpiler across builders.

Tools

Quanifi · Apache NiFi · OpenQASM 2.0 · Qiskit, Cirq, Qrisp, pyQuil, PennyLane · IBM, IQM, and Quantum Inspire backends

Abstract

Quantum computing has in recent years evolved from a purely theoretical field to an active area in both academia and industry. As a result, Quantum Software Engineering has emerged as an area that aims to organize the process of building, testing, and running quantum software. However, writing quantum software still requires programming with quantum gates and qubits, as well as knowledge specific to quantum software frameworks such as Qiskit, Cirq, Qrisp, pyQuil and PennyLane, each of which reaches quantum hardware through its own toolchain. We present Quanifi, which packages the high-level routines of these frameworks as components on the Apache NiFi dataflow canvas. The components exchange circuits as OpenQASM 2.0, so a circuit built by one framework can be executed by another. This allows for two types of redundancy: several frameworks implement the same algorithm, and several engines (simulators or real hardware) execute the same circuit. We describe N×M program execution, which crosses the two: a single NiFi flow runs each of the N implementations on each of the M engines, and because every result is labelled with its implementation and its engine, a disagreement can be linked to an implementation, to an engine, or to a single implementation-engine pair. We ran Grover's algorithm built by three frameworks on three quantum computers from IBM, IQM and Quantum Inspire, and a matrix of three adder builders on one IQM device reached through two routes. N×M execution helped us discover three real defects: an incorrect gate-set declaration in the Quantum Inspire adapter, execution consistent with negated R_x angles on Tuna-17, and circuit modification through Open Quantum. The latter two returned wrong answers without reporting an error. We reported all three defects and Open Quantum's provider confirmed and fixed its QASM parsing defect.
